accepted.question_text: Let an abelian square be a factor uv of a finite word such that u and v have the same Parikh vector, and let two abelian squares be considered distinct when they are different factor strings. Suppose a word of length n over an arbitrary alphabet contains k distinct abelian square factors. Must there always exist a binary word of the same length n that contains at least k distinct abelian square factors?
accepted.context_brief: Maximum distinct abelian squares across alphabet sizes

evidence.quote: Conjecture 0.1. If a word of length n contains k many distinct abelian square factors, then there exists a binary word of length n containing at least k many distinct abelian square factors.

accepted.question_text: For binary words of length n, let XNL(n) denote the maximum possible number of pairwise non-equivalent abelian square factors, where an abelian square is a factor uv with matching Parikh vectors and two abelian squares are non-equivalent when their Parikh vectors differ. Is XNL(n) always bounded above by a constant multiple of n^1.5?
accepted.context_brief: Maximum non-equivalent abelian squares in binary words

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an infinite word over a three-letter alphabet in which every abelian square has length exactly 2? Equivalently, is there an infinite ternary word containing no abelian square of length greater than two, so that the only possible abelian square types are the one-letter doubles aa, bb, and cc?
accepted.context_brief: Avoiding long abelian squares on three letters

evidence.quote: Conjecture 0.3. There exist infinite ternary words containing no abelian squares of length greater than two (which implies there are at most three distinct abelian squares).

accepted.question_text: For a binary linear word of length n, let MDL(n) be the minimum possible number of distinct abelian square factors. Is MDL(n) always equal to floor(n/4)? In addition, when n = 4k + 3, are the only binary words that attain exactly k distinct abelian squares the word a^(2k+1) b a^(2k+1) and its complement?
accepted.context_brief: Minimum distinct abelian squares in binary linear words

accepted.question_text: For a binary circular word of length n, let the count ignore abelian squares longer than the word itself, and let two abelian squares be considered distinct when they are different factor strings. Is the minimum number of distinct abelian square factors equal to (n - 1)/2 when n is odd and to (n - 2)/2 when n is even? Moreover, in the odd case are the only extremal circular words the conjugates and complements of a^n and a^(n-1)b, and in the even case are the only extremal circular words the conjugates and complements of a^k b^(n-k) with odd k?
accepted.context_brief: Minimum distinct abelian squares in binary circular words

accepted.question_text: Among all binary words of length n, what is the minimum possible total number of occurrences of abelian squares, where occurrences are counted with multiplicity rather than up to distinctness or equivalence?
accepted.context_brief: Minimum total abelian-square occurrences in binary words
